topic: Why India Is Stranger Than You Think
hook: Your sunrise in Arunachal comes long before Mumbai, yet both use the same clock.
title: Why India Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
India has one clock for a country so wide that the sun rises almost two hours earlier in the east. This video shows seven true facts: Assam's tea-garden time, Kanyakumari's two seas, rice farming below sea level in Kuttanad, living root bridges, a floating national park and a coal fire that has burned since 1916.

#India #IndiaFacts #StrangePlaces

chapters.title: The fire that never went out

scenes.narration: Your sunrise in Arunachal comes long before Mumbai, yet both use the same clock.
scenes.headline: One Clock, Two Suns

scenes.narration: That is the first of seven strange facts about India, and every single one is true.
scenes.headline: Seven True Facts

scenes.narration: By the end, you will see ground that has been on fire for more than a hundred years.
scenes.headline: Ground On Fire

scenes.narration: Then you will meet a bridge that is alive, and a national park that floats on water.
scenes.headline: Alive And Floating

scenes.narration: Stay until the last one, because the strangest place is the one with smoke rising from the ground.
scenes.headline: Save The Best

scenes.narration: First, look at how wide India is, from Gujarat in the west to Arunachal Pradesh in the far east.
scenes.headline: A Very Wide Country

scenes.narration: The whole country runs on one clock, Indian Standard Time, even though the sun rises almost two hours earlier in the east.
scenes.headline: One Time Zone

scenes.narration: In Arunachal, it can be bright morning while people in Gujarat are still waiting for first light.
scenes.headline: Bright In The East

scenes.narration: Offices and schools in both places open at nearly the same clock time, so the east loses daylight every morning.
scenes.headline: Same Opening Time

scenes.narration: The sun also sets earlier in the east, so evenings there turn dark while the clock still says afternoon.
scenes.headline: Early Sunsets

scenes.narration: A separate time zone for the north-east has been suggested for years, but the whole country still follows one clock.
scenes.headline: A Second Zone?

scenes.narration: Now here is the twist. Some places in India quietly decided to run on their own time.
scenes.headline: Their Own Time

scenes.narration: In Assam's tea gardens, the clock is one hour ahead of the rest of India.
scenes.headline: Assam Tea Time

scenes.narration: It is called Bagan time, and it started in British days so workers could use the early daylight.
scenes.headline: Bagan Time

scenes.narration: Garden workers begin and end their day by that clock, while the town nearby follows Indian Standard Time.
scenes.headline: Two Clocks, One District

scenes.narration: So two people in the same district can both say ten o'clock and mean different moments.
scenes.headline: Ten O'Clock Twice

scenes.narration: Ask for a time in Assam, and you may have to ask which clock they mean.
scenes.headline: Which Clock?

scenes.narration: That is strange enough, but the next place is where India itself runs out of land.
scenes.headline: Where India Ends

scenes.narration: At Kanyakumari, the southern tip of India, you can watch the sun rise and set over the sea from the same shore.
scenes.headline: Kanyakumari

scenes.narration: The Bay of Bengal lies on one side, the Arabian Sea on the other, and the Indian Ocean in front.
scenes.headline: Three Waters Meet

scenes.narration: In the morning the sun climbs out of the water, and in the evening it drops back into water.
scenes.headline: Sun In, Sun Out

scenes.narration: On the full moon day of Chaitra, crowds gather because the sun sets and the moon rises almost together.
scenes.headline: Sun And Moon

scenes.narration: The meeting of the waters also makes it a famous spot for pilgrims and tourists from across the country.
scenes.headline: A Famous Meeting Point

scenes.narration: Most coastlines give you a sunrise or a sunset over the sea, but rarely both from one place.
scenes.headline: Rare On Any Coast

scenes.narration: So the country ends with an ocean at its feet, and the next fact is about farming below the sea.
scenes.headline: Below The Sea

scenes.narration: In Kuttanad in Kerala, farmers grow rice in fields that sit below sea level.
scenes.headline: Kuttanad, Kerala

scenes.narration: Very few places in the world farm rice this way, and it only works because of long earth walls.
scenes.headline: Walls Hold Back Water

scenes.narration: In some places the water in the canal sits higher than the fields next to it.
scenes.headline: Water Above Fields

scenes.narration: Boats move between homes and rice fields here, and the backwaters work like roads for the villagers.
scenes.headline: Roads Made Of Water

scenes.narration: A barrage keeps salt water from the sea out of the fields, so the rice can grow.
scenes.headline: Keeping Salt Out

scenes.narration: Fields are drained before planting, and farmers here work on land that is wet for much of the year.
scenes.headline: Wet Farm Life

scenes.narration: If you like strange places like this, subscribe, because there are more of them coming.
scenes.headline: More Strange Places

scenes.narration: Next, a bridge that nobody built with bricks, because its builder was a tree.
scenes.headline: A Tree Builds A Bridge

scenes.narration: In Meghalaya, there are living bridges, grown from the roots of rubber fig trees.
scenes.headline: Living Bridges

scenes.narration: The Khasi people guide the roots across a river and tie them in place, then wait for them to thicken.
scenes.headline: Roots Guided Across

scenes.narration: It takes many years, and in some places decades, before a living bridge is strong enough to walk on.
scenes.headline: Decades To Grow

scenes.narration: A wooden or steel bridge can rot or rust in the heavy rain there, but a living one keeps growing stronger.
scenes.headline: Stronger With Age

scenes.narration: Some of these bridges are said to be hundreds of years old, and people still use them today.
scenes.headline: Still In Use

scenes.narration: Near Nongriat, there is even a double-decker root bridge, with two living bridges stacked over one stream.
scenes.headline: Double-Decker Bridge

scenes.narration: Cherrapunji is nearby, one of the wettest places on earth, and that rain is why these roots grow so well.
scenes.headline: Cherrapunji Rain

scenes.narration: Now imagine a national park that floats. That one is in Manipur, and it has a rare deer.
scenes.headline: A Park That Floats

scenes.narration: Loktak Lake in Manipur has floating islands called phumdis, made of soil, plants and rotting plant matter.
scenes.headline: Floating Islands

scenes.narration: Some are thick enough to hold huts, and fishing families live and work on them.
scenes.headline: Homes On Water

scenes.narration: One large phumdi forms Keibul Lamjao National Park, the only floating national park in the world.
scenes.headline: Only One On Earth

scenes.narration: It is home to the sangai, a rare deer that lives in the wild only in this park.
scenes.headline: The Sangai Deer

scenes.narration: Its hooves are suited to soft, marshy ground, so it can walk on the floating land.
scenes.headline: Made For Marsh

scenes.narration: The park rises and sinks with the changing water level, so the ground is never fixed.
scenes.headline: Ground That Moves

scenes.narration: Fishermen paddle small boats between the floating patches, and the lake is their main source of living.
scenes.headline: A Fishing Lake

scenes.narration: Floating land is strange, but the last place is stranger, because the ground there is burning.
scenes.headline: Now It Gets Worse

scenes.narration: In Jharia, Jharkhand, coal under the ground has been burning since 1916.
scenes.headline: Jharia Burns

scenes.narration: That is more than a hundred years of fire, and it still has not been put out.
scenes.headline: 100+ Years Of Fire

scenes.narration: Smoke rises from cracks in the earth, and in some places you can feel the heat from the ground.
scenes.headline: Smoke From Cracks

scenes.narration: Mining opened the coal to air, and air getting in through cracks and old workings keeps the fire alive.
scenes.headline: Air Feeds The Fire

scenes.narration: Families live close to the smoke, and the ground can sink as the coal underneath burns away.
scenes.headline: Homes Near The Smoke

scenes.narration: People have talked about moving residents for years, but many stay because their work and homes are right there.
scenes.headline: Why People Stay

scenes.narration: So here is a place where a fire has outlived generations, and the ground itself still smokes.
scenes.headline: A Fire Older Than Many

scenes.narration: Now go back to the start. Arunachal's sun rises before Mumbai's, yet one clock rules both.
scenes.headline: Back To The Start

scenes.narration: One clock, tea on its own time, an ocean sunrise, rice below the sea, living bridges, floating land, burning ground.
scenes.headline: The Full List

scenes.narration: All seven are real, and all seven are on the Indian map.
scenes.headline: All Seven Are Real

scenes.narration: Tomorrow: the Indian river island that is slowly disappearing into the water around it.
scenes.headline: Tomorrow: Majuli
